records.our_prose: Bell pepper is a warm-season vegetable in the same family as tomatoes and eggplant, grown for its sweet, blocky fruit. The nice thing about peppers is you can pick them at two stages: green and full-size, or left on the plant to ripen to red, orange, yellow, or purple and turn sweeter. Peppers pollinate themselves, so one plant will fruit, and they love warmth, so you grow them from transplants set into warm soil once the nights are mild. They are only light feeders, so going heavy on fertilizer gives you a big leafy plant with few peppers. The two things to watch are blossom-end rot, a dark sunken spot on the bottom of the fruit caused by uneven watering, and sunscald, a pale burned patch on peppers left exposed to strong sun. In very hot weather the flowers drop and the plant stops setting fruit for a while, so in hot climates peppers are grown in spring and fall with a summer break. The main things to get right are warmth, steady and even watering with mulch, modest fertilizer, full sun, and rotating peppers away from where tomatoes, potatoes, or eggplant grew.

records.our_prose: Bell peppers can be picked at TWO stages, and the choice is yours. Most are harvested GREEN and full-size, once the fruit is firm, blocky, and has thick, glossy walls; you do not need to wait for color. Left on the plant, the same fruit ripens through to its final red, orange, yellow, or purple, growing noticeably sweeter and richer in vitamins over the next two to three weeks. Ripening on the plant ties up the plant's energy, so picking peppers green keeps it flowering and setting more, while letting fruit color up slows further production. Cut peppers with pruners or a knife leaving a short stub of stem, rather than pulling, because the branches are brittle and snap easily. Harvest green types regularly, and watch colored fruit for anthracnose and sunscald if you leave it to ripen in hot, wet, or intensely sunny weather.

records.our_prose: Bell peppers like rich, well-drained soil that warms up in the sun, since they are warm-season plants that dislike cold, soggy ground. Mix in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting. If your soil is heavy clay or slow to warm, a sheet of black plastic or fabric mulch laid down before planting warms the soil and gives peppers the head start they want. Aim for soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged, because uneven watering is what causes the dark, sunken blossom-end rot on the bottom of the fruit.

records.our_prose: Midday wilting that recovers by evening is common in heat and not alarming, but leaves that stay limp signal real drought. The clearest sign of uneven watering is blossom-end rot: a dark, sunken, leathery patch on the blossom end of the fruit, caused not by a soil calcium shortage as such but by the plant's inability to move calcium to the fruit when moisture swings. Drought during flowering also drops blossoms and gives small fruit.

Iowa State puts good-management yields at roughly 15 to 20 pounds per 10-foot row.
